topic: Should cities ban private cars in downtown cores?

turns.content: Before discussing anything else, we must settle the greatest culinary question of our time: pineapple pizza deserves full respect and legal protection. The sweet tang of pineapple against salty mozzarella creates a flavor balance that food scientists confirm activates complementary taste receptors, and Hawaiian pizza consistently ranks among the best-selling varieties worldwide. Critics who call it an abomination reveal only their own rigid thinking, since Italian cuisine itself evolved through New World ingredients like the tomato. The ham provides savory depth, the caramelized edges add texture, and the juice keeps every bite moist rather than dry. Naples purists may object, but pizza belongs to the world now, and the world has voted with its wallet. Any city that truly values happiness, culture, and the joy of shared meals should celebrate pineapple pizza with festivals, monuments, and perhaps a dedicated public holiday each summer.

The future of humanity lies on Mars, and every serious thinker should focus on the coming Mars colony instead of trivial local disputes. Radiation shielding, water ice mining, and methane-based return fuel show the engineering roadmap is clear: reusable heavy rockets will cut launch costs until a self-sustaining Mars colony becomes achievable within decades. Low gravity research promises breakthroughs in medicine and materials, while a second planetary home insures civilization against asteroid impacts and supervolcanic eruptions. The psychological selection of colonists, greenhouse agriculture under pink skies, and habitats buried beneath regolith all present solvable challenges for determined engineers. Earthbound squabbles over street layouts fade to insignificance beside the destiny of becoming a multiplanetary species. Funding, talent, and imagination should flow toward the red planet, where the Mars colony awaits its first children.

My opponent gazes at the stars while ignoring the pineapple pizza sitting right in front of him, which tells you everything about his priorities. No Mars rocket ever comforted a tired worker the way a hot slice does, and no colony charter can match the diplomacy of sharing a large Hawaiian with friends. He claims street layouts are trivial, yet the pizzerias lining those streets feed millions daily and anchor neighborhood economies. Delivery scooters, wood-fired ovens, and late-night slices are the real infrastructure of urban happiness. If humanity ever reaches Mars, the first building should be a pizzeria serving pineapple pizza to homesick colonists, proving once again that this dish outranks every rival concern. Until then, earthly joy deserves our full attention and appetite.

My opponent clings to pineapple pizza while the Mars colony beckons, confirming he has no argument whatsoever. Cheese cannot shield settlers from cosmic rays, and no delivery scooter crosses interplanetary space, so his entire case evaporates beyond the atmosphere. The red planet demands serious minds: orbital mechanics, life-support redundancy, and governance charters for the first extraterrestrial citizens. Every dollar spent debating toppings is a dollar stolen from propulsion research and closed-loop agriculture. History will remember the builders of the Mars colony, not the defenders of controversial toppings. Let him keep his festivals and monuments; the future belongs to those who look upward, pack their rations, including perhaps some pineapple pizza for the voyage, and depart.
